Juan]]|[[FIBA Americas Championship 1999|Team competition]]}} }} '''Richard Clay''' "'''Rip'''" '''Hamilton''' (born February 14, 1978) is an American former professional [[basketball]] player and current basketball analyst for [[CBS Sports HQ]]. Hamilton played 14 seasons in the [[National Basketball Association]] (NBA) and is best known for his nine-year stint with the [[Detroit Pistons]], where he was a three-time [[NBA All-Star Game|All-Star]]. He helped lead the Pistons to six straight Eastern Conference Finals appearances, back to back NBA Finals appearances, their best record in franchise history (64–18 in [[2005–06 Detroit Pistons season|2005–06]]) and the [[2004 NBA Finals|2004 NBA championship]]. Born and raised in [[Coatesville, Pennsylvania]], a city {{Convert|40|mi|km|abbr=out}} west of [[Philadelphia]], Hamilton played [[college basketball]] for three years with the [[UConn Huskies men's basketball|UConn Huskies]]. In his [[1999 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament|third and final year]], Hamilton was named the [[NCAA basketball tournament Most Outstanding Player|Final Four's Most Outstanding Player]] en route to an upset [[1999 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament|NCAA Championship]] win over the favored [[1998–99 Duke Blue Devils men's basketball team|Duke Blue Devils]]. He is the [[List of Connecticut Huskies men's basketball players with 1000 points|second-leading scorer in Connecticut Huskies history]]. Named a consensus first-team [[1999 NCAA Men's Basketball All-Americans|All-American]], Hamilton decided to forgo his senior year and enter the [[1999 NBA draft|NBA draft]]. Drafted seventh overall by the [[Washington Wizards]] where he would spend the next three seasons, Hamilton notably averaged 20 points per game starting next to [[Michael Jordan]]. Traded to Detroit for [[Jerry Stackhouse]] in 2002, Hamilton played with the Pistons for nine seasons before ending his career with two final seasons with the [[Chicago Bulls]]. The Pistons retired his No. 32 jersey on February 26, 2017.

'''Walter Ray Allen Jr.''' (born July 20, 1975) is an American former professional [[basketball]] player. Allen played 18 seasons in the [[National Basketball Association]] (NBA) and was inducted into the [[Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame]] as a player in 2018. He is widely considered one of the greatest [[Three-point field goal|three-point]] shooters of all time. Allen was a ten-time [[NBA All-Star Game|NBA All-Star]], and won an [[gold medal|Olympic gold medal]] as a member of the [[2000 United States men's Olympic basketball team|2000 United States men's basketball team]]. At the time of his retirement, he was the [[List of NBA career 3-point scoring leaders|leading three-point scorer in NBA history]] until he was surpassed by [[Stephen Curry]] in 2021. As of 2025, he ranks third on the NBA's all-time three-pointers list. In 2021, he was selected to the [[NBA 75th Anniversary Team]].

Allen played [[college basketball]] for the [[Connecticut Huskies men's basketball|Connecticut Huskies]] for three seasons, before he was selected with the fifth overall pick in the [[1996 NBA draft]], and developed into a prolific scorer for the [[Milwaukee Bucks]], featuring alongside [[Glenn Robinson]] and [[Sam Cassell]] as the team achieved playoff success. In 2003, he was traded to the [[Seattle SuperSonics]], where he solidified his reputation as a scorer, breaking several league records for [[Three-point field goal|three-point]] and [[free throw]] shooting. Allen was later traded to the [[Boston Celtics]], where he formed a "Big Three" with [[Kevin Garnett]] and [[Paul Pierce]]; the team won an NBA championship in [[2008 NBA Finals|2008]]. After five seasons with the Celtics, he played with the [[Miami Heat]] for two seasons, reaching the [[NBA Finals]] both times and winning the title in [[2013 NBA Finals|2013]]; his clutch three-pointer to force overtime in Game 6 of the 2013 Finals is regarded as one of the most iconic and memorable plays in NBA history. Allen retired on November 1, 2016, after playing for four different teams.

During his NBA career, Allen acted in some films, such as his role as basketball prodigy Jesus Shuttlesworth in [[Spike Lee]]'s basketball drama ''[[He Got Game]]'' (1998). Allen's performance as Shuttlesworth was praised by critics, and the name was borrowed as Allen's basketball nickname.<ref>{{cite news|first=Emanuel|last=Levy|url=https://variety.com/1998/film/reviews/he-got-game-1117477426/|title=He Got Game|work=Variety|date=1998-04-27|access-date=2020-02-26|archive-date=March 10, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220310235258/https://variety.com/1998/film/reviews/he-got-game-1117477426/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="suntimes1">{{cite news|url=https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/he-got-game-1998|title=He Got Game|first=Roger|last=Ebert|website=Rogerebert.com|date=May 1, 1998|access-date=February 26, 2020|archive-date=August 31, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220831042423/https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/he-got-game-1998|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Edelstein |first=David |url=https://slate.com/culture/1998/05/he-got-balls.html|title=He Got Balls |work=Slate|date=1998-05-03 |access-date=2020-02-26|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090125225131/http://slate.msn.com/id/3252 |archive-date=2009-01-25 }}</ref>

Over his career, Felton was a member of the [[Charlotte Bobcats]], [[New York Knicks]] (twice), [[Denver Nuggets]], [[Portland Trail Blazers]], [[Dallas Mavericks]], [[Los Angeles Clippers]] and [[Oklahoma City Thunder]]. He played the [[point guard]] position.

He became the youngest player ever to play in the Spanish [[Liga ACB]] on 15 October 2005, at age 14.<ref name=":0">{{cite web|title=Ricky Rubio establece un nuevo récord al debutar en la ACB con catorce años|url=http://www.libertaddigital.com/php3/noticia.php3?cpn=1276263122|work=Libertad Digital|date=15 October 2005|access-date=14 August 2006|language=es|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070312042248/http://www.libertaddigital.com/php3/noticia.php3?cpn=1276263122|archive-date=12 March 2007}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{cite magazine|first=Marty|last=Burns|title=NBA types will have their eyes on Spanish phenom Rubio at Olympics|url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/2008/writers/marty_burns/08/07/rubio.olympics/|magazine=[[Sports Illustrated]]|date=8 August 2008|access-date=8 August 2008|archive-date=26 October 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121026114826/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/2008/writers/marty_burns/08/07/rubio.olympics/|url-status=dead}}</ref> Rubio made his [[EuroLeague]] debut on 24 October 2006, a few days after turning 16,<ref>{{cite web|title=Report - Welcome to EUROLEAGUE BASKETBALL|url=https://www.euroleague.net/main/results/showgame/report?pcode=LFW&gamecode=7&seasoncode=E2006|website=Euroleague.net|date=21 May 2023|access-date=21 May 2023}}</ref> making him [[List of youngest EuroLeague players since the 2000–01 season|one of the youngest players to play in the EuroLeague]].

On 25 June 2009, Rubio was drafted with the fifth pick in the first round of the [[2009 NBA draft]] by the [[Minnesota Timberwolves]],<ref>NBA.com, [http://www.nba.com/timberwolves/news/Timberwolves_Select_Ricky_Rubio_at_No5-090625.html Wolves Select Ricky Rubio at No. 5], accessed 20 July 2009.</ref> making him the first player born in the 1990s to be drafted by an NBA team. The Timberwolves had an agreement in principle with his Spanish team, [[Joventut Badalona|DKV Joventut]], to buy out his contract, but Rubio backed out of the deal.<ref name="Backing out">{{cite news|title=Kahn: Rubio not ready to jump to NBA|url=https://www.espn.com/nba/news/story?id=4437300|website=ESPN.com|date=1 September 2009|access-date=1 September 2009}}</ref> On 31 August 2009, Joventut traded the rights to Rubio to [[FC Barcelona Bàsquet|FC Barcelona]],<ref name="Rubio to Barça">{{cite news|first1=Ric|last1=Bucher|first2=Chris|last2=Sheridan|title=Sources: Wolves can't work buyout|url=https://www.espn.com/nba/news/story?id=4435861|name-list-style=amp|work=ESPN|date=31 August 2009|access-date=1 September 2009}}</ref> and Rubio signed a six-year contract with FC Barcelona the following day.<ref name="Barça signing">{{cite web|title=REGAL FCB scores teen sensation Rubio|url=http://www.euroleague.net/euroleaguenews/transactions/2009-10-signings/i/55545/3694/regal-fcb-scores-teen-sensation-ricky-rubio|publisher=[[Euroleague]]|date=1 September 2009|access-date=1 September 2009}}</ref> In 2011, Rubio joined the Timberwolves,<ref name="wojnarowski1">{{cite news|first=Adrian|last=Wojnarowski|title=Sources: Rubio, T'wolves reach deal|url=https://sports.yahoo.com/nba/news?slug=aw-wojnarowski_ricky_rubio_deal_timberwolves_060111 |work=Yahoo! Sports|date=1 June 2011|access-date=1 June 2011}}</ref> and spent six seasons in Minnesota before being traded to the [[Utah Jazz]] in June 2017. He signed with the [[Phoenix Suns]] in July 2019, before returning to Minnesota in 2020. Rubio was traded to the [[Cleveland Cavaliers]] in August 2021, but was dealt to the [[Indiana Pacers]] a month after suffering a season ending ACL injury in December.

In August 2023, Rubio announced he was taking a break from the sport to prioritise his mental health. In January 2024, he announced that he would be retiring from the NBA.
